title: Organising Writing into Paragraphs
keyIdea: A paragraph is a group of sentences about one idea. Start a new paragraph when the idea changes, not after a set number of sentences, so a paragraph can be two sentences or five. In a story, start a new paragraph for a new time, place, topic or person speaking (TiPToP). In non-fiction, a title names the whole topic, a sub-heading names one paragraph, and a topic sentence at the start tells the reader what the paragraph is about.

kid: A paragraph is a group of sentences about one idea. In a report on hedgehogs, one paragraph can tell what they look like, the next what they eat, and the next where they live. Each sentence goes with the others about the same idea.

Start a new paragraph when the idea changes. There is no set number of lines. If you write two sentences about a fox's fur and four about its food, that is two paragraphs: one short and one long. On the page, a new paragraph starts on a new line, often set in a little or after a gap.

Stories use paragraphs too. Remember TiPToP: start a new one for a new Time, a new Place, a new Topic, which is something new that happens, or a new Person speaking. Each time someone new speaks, they get a new line.

Information texts can also use headings. The title names the whole topic, like Bats. A sub-heading is a short label for one part, like Food. It is not a full sentence. Open each paragraph with a topic sentence that tells the reader what it is about, then add the details.
adult: This is the Key Stage 2 writing work on paragraphs in the national curriculum for England. In Years 3 and 4 pupils organise paragraphs around a theme, and the grammar appendix introduces paragraphs as a way to group related material. In non-narrative writing they use simple organisational devices such as headings and sub-headings. In Years 5 and 6 they build cohesion within and across paragraphs and use further devices to structure text.

Useful terms: paragraph, theme, related material, heading or title, sub-heading, topic sentence and indent. TiPToP (time, place, topic, person) is a common classroom memory aid for when a story needs a new paragraph. The rule for speech is the firmest: each new speaker gets a new paragraph.

Common mistakes: breaking after a set number of lines, or writing one long block. Mixing two themes in one paragraph, such as a hedgehog's food among facts about its home. Using a full sentence or the whole topic name as a sub-heading. Keeping a new speaker's words in the last speaker's paragraph. Opening with a detail instead of saying what the paragraph is about.

In the lab your child sorts six hedgehog sentences into three themed paragraphs, then marks the breaks in a fox report that has no paragraphs and finds they fall after two sentences and after six. They give the TiPToP reason for four breaks in a river story, place a title and three sub-headings over a bat page (one card is a sentence, not a heading) and choose the topic sentence that opens a paragraph.

familyTip: When your child writes a few lines about a day out or a pet, ask them to say the one idea each paragraph is about. If a sentence is about something else, does it need a paragraph of its own?

visual.caption: Which paragraph does it belong in? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: A pointed nose and small eyes
Short legs and a tiny tail
Under a hedge or a shed

lab.caption: Flagship lab: group hedgehog facts, mark the breaks in a fox report, give TiPToP reasons, place sub-headings and pick topic sentences.

practice.prompt: When should you start a new paragraph in a report?
practice.hint: Think about what a paragraph is about: one idea.
practice.explain: A paragraph keeps to one idea, so a new paragraph starts when the idea changes, however long the last one was.

practice.prompt: A report has {a} sentences about a dog's looks, then {b} sentences about its food. How many paragraphs should it have?
practice.hint: Count the ideas, not the sentences.
practice.explain: There are two ideas, looks and food, so the {=a+b} sentences make 2 paragraphs.

practice.prompt: In a story: "The next day, Leo went back to the cave." Why does this start a new paragraph?
practice.hint: Look at the first three words.
practice.explain: "The next day" moves the story to a new time, the T in TiPToP.

practice.prompt: A story has {n} lines of speech, and each line is said by a different person from the line before. How many new paragraphs do those lines start?
practice.hint: Each new speaker gets a new paragraph.
practice.explain: Every change of speaker starts a new paragraph, so {n} lines of speech start {n} paragraphs.

pool.prompt: Which is the best sub-heading for a paragraph about where owls live?
choices: Owls live in barns and trees.
pool.hint: A sub-heading is a short label for one part, not a sentence.
pool.explain: Homes is a short label for that one paragraph. A full sentence is not a heading, and Owls names the whole report, so it is the title.

pool.prompt: Which sentence should open a paragraph about how frogs breathe?
choices: Frogs can breathe in two ways.
They take in air through their skin.
pool.hint: Pick the sentence that tells what the whole paragraph is about.
pool.explain: "Frogs can breathe in two ways" is the topic sentence. The skin fact is a detail, and frog eggs belong in another paragraph.

pool.prompt: A paragraph about what cats eat has one sentence about where cats sleep. What should you do?
choices: Move it to a paragraph about sleep
pool.hint: Each paragraph keeps to one idea.
pool.explain: The sleep sentence is about a different idea, so it belongs in its own paragraph about where cats sleep.

pool.prompt: "Meanwhile, back at the castle, the queen was waiting." Which TiPToP reasons start this paragraph?
pool.hint: Look for when and where words.
pool.explain: "Meanwhile" signals a change of time and "back at the castle" a change of place, so it needs a new paragraph.

pool.prompt: A report on sharks has the title Sharks and {n} paragraphs, each with its own sub-heading. How many headings are there in all, counting the title?
pool.hint: One title, plus one sub-heading for each paragraph.

pool.prompt: Amy says, "Can I come?" Then Raj answers, "Yes, hurry!" How should Raj's words be set out?
choices: On a new line, in a new paragraph
In the same paragraph as Amy
pool.hint: What happens each time a new person speaks?
pool.explain: Raj is a new speaker, so his words start a new paragraph. Stories do not usually use sub-headings.

pool.prompt: Which reason is NOT a good reason to start a new paragraph?
choices: The last paragraph had four sentences
The story moves to a new place
pool.explain: Length is not a reason on its own. A new place, time, event or speaker is.

pool.prompt: Your report on bees has {a} sentences about their bodies, {b} about making honey and {c} about the hive. If each idea gets one paragraph, how many paragraphs are there?
pool.hint: Count the ideas: bodies, honey, hive.
pool.explain: Three ideas make 3 paragraphs, even though there are {=a+b+c} sentences in all.
